newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE-Mall new arena for Israel's religious battles.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Mall new arena for Israel's religious battles.

text.p: If you can't beat them, buy them.
That's how some Israelis view efforts by an ultra-religious Jew to keep a shopping mall being built in the epicentre of secular Israel from opening on the sabbath.
For decades, orthodox Jews have twisted political arms of Israel's secular majority to force public religious observance. But millionaire Lev Leviev hit on a new strategy.
He simply bought the mall.
Leviev paid $141 million last November for a controlling stake in Africa Israel, the company developing the shopping centre in Tel Aviv's upmarket Ramat Aviv neighbourhood.
Last month he announced the doors would be locked every Friday evening until sundown on Saturday -- the day of rest according to Jewish law.
While most shops in Israel close for the sabbath, movie theatres and restaurants remain open and do much of their business on the weekends.
"It's an assault on our secular lifestyle in Tel Aviv. He's cynically using his money in order to force people to live his way," said Tel Aviv Deputy Mayor Dan Darin.
The sabbath policy only adds fuel to the fire for secular Jews who complain of "religious coercion" in Israel.

Under "status quo" understandings dating back to the state's founding in 1948, buses do not run on the sabbath, streets are barricaded in religious neighbourhoods, and ritual ceremonies such as weddings and funerals are the domain of orthodox rabbis.
Even the national airline El Al flies only six days a week.
ACTING ACCORDING TO HIS FAITH

Leviev, 40, lives in Belgium most of the year but owns a home in Tel Aviv's ultra-orthodox suburb of Bnei Brak where men in black coats and side-curls and women in religious head coverings sit separately on buses and in restaurants.
He made much of his fortune, estimated at more than $500 million, in the diamond business and says financial considerations alone governed his decision to buy Africa Israel.
"Mr Leviev is a religious man and he acts according to his faith. In this case, that means closing the mall on the sabbath," said a company spokeswoman.
Shareholders have voiced dismay. Africa Israel share prices have dipped by as much as 25 percent since Leviev bought it.

But Leviev says Jews who observe religious rituals -- including dietary laws and the commandment to rest on the sabbath -- will visit the mall in droves on weekdays to support his policy of closing the shopping centre on the sabbath.
"People forget who owns this shopping mall," Leviev told the Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper in a recent interview.
"I paid for it (the mall) and no one else...My businesses won't run on the sabbath and I will take that battle to court if I have to."
"THIS IS NOT TEHRAN"
No place in Israel contrasts more sharply with Bnei Brak than Ramat Aviv, adjacent to hip Tel Aviv university where mini-skirts and navel rings abound.
The mall is a stone's throw from the homes of ultra-secular legislator Yossi Sarid and former prime ministers Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres, both of the left-centre Labour party.
Many Ramat Aviv residents opposed construction of the mall -- a cement eyesore overshadowing quaint three-storey apartment buildings and tidy lawns -- long before Leviev bought it.
But keeping it open on weekends has become a rallying cry.
Dozens of women protested last month near the construction site wearing black veils and chanting: "This is not Tehran".
The reference to Iran has become a theme. Nehamia Strasler, the business editor of Israel's Haaretz newspaper, nicknamed Leviev "The Ayatollah of Ramat Aviv".
"I'm not too thrilled about the mall, but if it's going to be built, I don't want some outsider dictating when it will open and when it will close," said resident Noa Zuckerman, 22.
"LIKE BEING HANDCUFFED TO THEIR WORST ENEMY"
Leviev's chief opponents, McDonald's managing director in Israel, Omri Padan, and Mooky Greidinger of Israel Theatres, accuse the orthodox tycoon of reneging on signed agreements.

"The contract talks about operating the theatres seven days a week. I think they aren't exactly aware of all the details in the agreement," said Greidinger, adding that 80 percent of his revenue comes from movies screened on weekends.
Padan says his contract with Africa Israel, signed before Leviev bought the company, allows him to open a non-kosher McDonald's in the shopping centre.
He has refused to "go kosher" -- as some McDonald's restaurants have in Israel -- despite Leviev's offer to make the fast-food chain the only hamburger restaurant in the mall.
Other business owners hope neighbourhood pressure will force Africa Israel to keep the shopping centre open on weekends but no one is talking about pulling out even if Leviev gets his way.
"Nobody is going to pull out no matter what happens because this is a very lucrative situation. It's a huge mall in the heart of a high-income population," the businessman said.
"For some of the business owners it's like being handcuffed to their worst enemy. They'll just have to figure out a way to get along."
